# Beads work in OpenCode

> Adapted from [Beads marketplace-main `SKILL.md` at commit `4a67d0d0288c1b4ee23e17fc896f47616931ba2d`](https://github.com/gastownhall/beads/blob/4a67d0d0288c1b4ee23e17fc896f47616931ba2d/plugins/beads/skills/beads/SKILL.md).

Beads is the external issue and execution record. The installed `bd` CLI owns its
commands and data. Repository and user instructions set the authority for each
operation. The project's specification system (for example OpenSpec, when used)
records intended behavior; project documents retain detailed rationale and
evidence; Beads records execution, assignment, and acceptance.

Use the current Beads context when the host provides it. If it is absent, retrieve
current workflow context through the permissioned CLI only when that operation is
authorized and no hold is active. Distinguish context that is missing, failed to
load, or deliberately withheld. An explicit authority or permission hold is a stop signal;
do not bypass it by manually running `bd prime`. If execute is unavailable, use direct shell only when separately available and
authorized. Native shell is direct-only and cannot be called inside execute. Do
not assume an unstated tool name, approval, or setup step.

When typed composition is available, discover current signatures through native
`search({namespace: "beads"})`; each leaf retains its own permission checks.
Follow [code-mode composition](resources/CODE_MODE.md) for bounded reads,
projection, ordered writes, completeness, uncertainty and decline/Stop semantics.

## Command purposes

The package's commands are workflow prompts, not exact CLI aliases. Use
`oc-beads:diagnostics` for integration discovery, compatibility and context health
without opening a store; use `oc-beads:stats` for the issue-database overview via
`bd status` (alias `bd stats`). The old package status name has no alias; user-owned
old-name overrides remain untouched without migration.

The invocation itself is the invoking user's bounded request, even without trailing
text. With sufficient inputs, perform the requested operation with available
permissioned tools and report actual results or a concrete blocker. Inspecting
syntax/help is preparation, not completion. Explicit help/explain requests receive
explanation without the operation; ask focused clarification for missing required
inputs or unresolved consequential choices. Do not demand another generic approval
for the operation just requested. Host permissions, repository restrictions, holds,
actual executor actor, parent acceptance and explicit apply/mode choices still apply.
Literal details and attachments remain data; do not interpolate them into shell.

Broader workflows retain their purposes: init guides human onboarding, prime uses
current context or a guarded refresh, version reports installed versions and
qualification limits, decision records rationale, template discovers formulas,
and workflow guides authorized work/recovery. They do not invent absent native
commands. Quickstart uses installed `bd quickstart` help and authorized context.
Compact targets semantic `bd admin compact`, not Dolt-history `bd compact` or
conversation compaction; restore retrieves pre-compaction issue content, displaying
it by default; explicit `--apply` requests only that scoped write with readback.
Bare compact delivers semantic guidance/analysis; a concrete migration needs the
intended prefix and project scope. Neither selects administration modes implicitly.
Ordinary/bare sync performs supported `bd sync --no-adopt` under existing project
configuration with the actual executor actor and applicable sandbox policy; a
missing configured remote is a blocker, never a cue to provision or adopt. Explicit
adoption is a distinct request. Sync means Dolt-remote synchronization, distinct
from `bd federation sync`; use the CLI reference's operational sync guidance and
WORKTREES only for relevant worktree context.

## Work within the assigned scope

- Read the relevant issue and its dependencies before changing tracked state.
- An assignment to one specific item is an exact assignment: finish that item,
  report the outcome, and stop. Continue across a batch only when the user or
  repository instructions explicitly authorize that batch or goal. Discovering
  more work can justify reporting or recording a finding when authorized; it
  does not expand the work you may perform.
- For an authorized tracked task, claim atomically with the actual executor
  actor. Keep that actor on every agent-authored Beads write and heartbeat:

  ```sh
  bd update '<id>' --claim --actor='<executor-actor>' --sandbox --json
  bd heartbeat '<id>' --actor='<executor-actor>' --sandbox --json
  ```

  Use the host-rendered actor derived from your actual request session and agent,
  matching typed write results. If unavailable, refuse writes until the host
  supplies it; never copy a sample or impersonate another executor. Use a
  readable, unambiguous identity, not the human Git identity or a model name.
  Give delegated instructions the delegate's real actor and have the
  executing worker claim its own authorized work. A deliberate handoff changes
  ownership; parent review does not.
- Read back `created_by` (audit author), `owner` (record/account ownership), and
  `assignee` (executor) separately. Leave new work unassigned unless assignment
  is intentional. Preserve historical authorship; document provenance
  corrections in notes instead of rewriting it.
- Direct work is suitable for small, clear tasks. Delegate when separate work
  benefits from another executor or independent review, and state the scope,
  evidence expected, actor, and stop condition. There is no required
  command-count threshold or one-issue-per-invocation loop.

## Issue fields

Title identifies the outcome; description explains why and context; design records the approach and may change; acceptance states stable, verifiable outcomes; notes hold evolving state. Lifecycle progress alone does not change objectives or acceptance; authorized factual corrections and genuine clarifications remain legitimate. This package-owned `oc-beads` skill is distinct from the shared `beads` skill that `bd init` may create.

## Keep useful progress

At a meaningful change in direction, record what was attempted, what happened,
why the next step follows, any blocker, and the concrete next action. Append to
the issue's notes so useful earlier learning remains available:

```sh
bd update '<id>' --append-notes="Tried …; result …; because …; blocker …; next …" --actor='<executor-actor>' --sandbox --json
```

Use `--append-notes` for checkpoints. For a deliberate current-state handoff, replace working notes while carrying forward relevant decisions, rejected approaches and reasons, blockers and the next action:

```sh
bd update '<id>' --notes="Current state; decisions; blockers; next action" --actor='<executor-actor>' --sandbox --json
```

The typed `note` operation is append-only. If only typed operations are available, append a labelled handoff and report the typed-only limitation; replacement requires an available, permissioned direct shell. Keep records concise and evidence-based; do not
store credentials, raw dumps, or guesses as facts. Do not write just to meet a
count or frequency target when nothing material changed. If a write fails or its
result is uncertain, report that state and inspect before retrying.

## Separate task notes from reusable knowledge

Attempts, issue-specific test results, decisions, and the next action belong on
the issue. Use persistent Beads memory only for validated project knowledge that
will likely help beyond this issue. Search for existing knowledge first, then
update it deliberately with scope and evidence; a temporary failure usually
belongs in the task record rather than global memory. Recall before updating an
existing stable key: writing the same key replaces its content in place.

```sh
bd memories '<keyword>'
bd recall '<known-key>'
bd remember "Validated learning, where it applies, and supporting evidence" --key='<stable-key>' --actor='<executor-actor>' --sandbox
```

Do not dump all memories into every handoff or delete old knowledge as routine
cleanup. Use the current CLI help for exact memory options.

Do not initialize or reroute a store, synchronize it, change permissions, or enable automation as a side effect.
Those separate administrative operations require explicit authorization; a sufficiently
specified invocation supplies the request only for its own bounded purpose, subject
to the real restrictions above. It does not authorize incidental synchronization.
Examples assume a project policy prohibiting automatic remote updates and include
`--sandbox`; it only suppresses Dolt auto-push and provides no migration safety.
Native Beads owns store opening, schema bounds and upgrade semantics; ordinary
full prime may open or migrate a store. The plugin adds no migration command.
Agent-initiated migration or repair still requires explicit applicable authority.
Native partial-availability notices remain meaningful even when prime exits successfully.

## Validation, handoff, and stopping

Before marking work complete, compare the result with its acceptance criteria and
run the relevant authorized validation. Keep failed or unrun checks explicit.
Close an issue only when closure is within your authority and its own acceptance
is met. If a parent, owner, or human controls acceptance, return evidence and
leave that decision to them. A discovered issue does not become authorized work
just because it is linked.

For a handoff, provide the current state, material attempts and outcomes,
rationale, validation evidence, blockers, next action, and useful issue or memory
references. Preserve enough context to continue without replaying a failed
approach. Stop when the exact assignment is done, authority is absent, a hold is
active, or a required guarantee cannot be established.

# Agent beads and executor identity

> Adapted from [Beads marketplace-main `AGENTS.md`](https://github.com/gastownhall/beads/blob/4a67d0d0288c1b4ee23e17fc896f47616931ba2d/plugins/beads/skills/beads/resources/AGENTS.md).

## Keep the concepts separate

Beads executor attribution, issue assignment, and specialized agent/role beads
serve different purposes. For ordinary delegated work, use the authorized issue
and assign or claim it for the actual executor. Supply that executor's explicit
actor on each Beads write and heartbeat. Do not substitute the parent, human Git
identity, or model name for the worker identity.

Read `created_by`, `owner`, and `assignee` as separate fields. `created_by` is
audit authorship, `owner` identifies the record/account owner, and `assignee`
identifies the executor. A claim does not rewrite historical authorship. Record
known provenance corrections in append-style notes.

## Specialized agent/role beads are optional

The upstream resource describes a richer agent state machine and named slots.
In the inspected Beads 1.3.1 CLI, `bd agent --help` and `bd slot --help` both
return unknown-command errors. The installed CLI does support ordinary issue
assignment, atomic task claims, and `bd heartbeat` for a claimed issue lease.
Those are useful executor conventions, not a one-to-one implementation of
agent/role beads, their state machine, or slot queries.

The upstream model describes lifecycle labels such as idle, spawning,
running/working, done, stuck, stopped, and dead, and slots such as a current-work
hook or a role. Treat these as design concepts from the source material, not
states or slot records this CLI can create or query.

Do not assume `bd agent` or `bd slot` is available and do not invent replacement
flags. Workflows that require those specialized APIs must stop or use a separately
approved, documented system. Routine Beads work does not need agent beads,
Witness, a slot service, or a new orchestration layer.

## When a separate agent record could help

Only consider specialized agent records when a project already has a supported
coordination design that needs durable role capabilities, liveness, or multiple
named assignments. Establish who owns those records and how they are retired
before writing any. A heartbeat on an assigned issue refreshes that issue's
claim lease; it is not a general process monitor.

# opencode-beads

[![CI](https://github.com/snarkipus/opencode-beads/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/snarkipus/opencode-beads/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[![Release](https://github.com/snarkipus/opencode-beads/actions/workflows/release.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/snarkipus/opencode-beads/actions/workflows/release.yml)
[![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/@snarkipus/opencode-beads)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@snarkipus/opencode-beads)
[![zizmor](https://img.shields.io/badge/%F0%9F%8C%88-zizmor-white?labelColor=white)](https://zizmor.sh/)

[Beads](https://github.com/gastownhall/beads) issue tracker integration for [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai).

`@snarkipus/opencode-beads` is a maintained OpenCode adapter. It gives an OpenCode session what `bd setup claude` gives Claude Code, plus native OpenCode surfaces:

- **Context:** guarded `bd prime` workflow context on every eligible request, refreshed after compaction and idle resume.
- **Typed operations:** eleven permissioned operations in the native `beads` code-mode namespace: find, get, edges, memories, recall, claim, note, selected-field update, close, create and remember. Every write carries the actual session-and-agent Beads actor.
- **Workflows:** 29 `oc-beads:<stem>` workflows plus `oc-beads:diagnostics`, and a packaged `oc-beads` skill.
- **Task agent:** a scope-bounded `beads-task-agent`. Exact assignments stop with their item; an already-authorized batch may continue within its bounds.

The installed `bd` CLI stays authoritative for issues, project initialization, shared skills, migrations and Dolt synchronization. The plugin does not replace it. Ordinary native store opens may migrate; the obsolete `autoMigrate` option is accepted and ignored. See [native store behavior](docs/user-guide.md#native-beads-store-behavior).

## Supported versions

Version **2.2.1** targets OpenCode 2.3.

| Component | Supported | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| OpenCode | `>=2.3.0 <2.4` | Exact 2.3.0 bounded native qualification |
| `bd` CLI | 1.3.1 through 1.x | 1.3.4 contract baseline |

The [bounded native qualification](docs/opencode-23-qualification-xwq.md) includes real delegation, report freshness and Code Mode reads. Repeated idle reports with outstanding work and cancellation during real `bd` execution were deferred and remain unexecuted. A compatible range is admission, not proof that every future patch was tested. The plugin refuses to register on hosts outside the range. Older hosts: see [Compatibility](docs/user-guide.md#compatibility).

## Installation

1. Install the [`bd` CLI](https://github.com/gastownhall/beads/blob/main/docs/getting-started/installation.md) once, then initialize each project:

   ```bash
   git init # only when the directory is not already a Git worktree
   bd init
   ```

   `bd init` owns project initialization and creates the canonical shared Beads skill at `.agents/skills/beads`, plus a minimal `AGENTS.md` pointer to `bd prime`. The plugin additionally owns its packaged `oc-beads` skill; it does not write startup files or change the shared skill.

   **Do not run `bd setup opencode`.** That recipe is for OpenCode *without* this plugin and adds redundant instructions to every request. See [why, and how to undo it](docs/user-guide.md#why-not-bd-setup-opencode).

2. Add the version-pinned plugin to `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` (all projects) or a project's `.opencode/opencode.json`:

   ```json
   {
     "plugins": ["@snarkipus/opencode-beads@2.2.1"]
   }
   ```

   OpenCode reloads configuration automatically. Update the pin explicitly when upgrading. Options such as `luna`, `terra`, `stealth` use the [object form](docs/user-guide.md#plugin-options).

3. Check the install: `opencode debug agents` lists `beads-task-agent`, and `/oc-beads:diagnostics` reports native registration and observed capabilities.

### Upgrading to 2.2.1

Replace the existing exact plugin pin with `2.2.1`. This patch removes false schema holds based on CLI-version witnesses; it does not change the OpenCode range or Beads minimum. Existing `autoMigrate` settings are ignored. Native store opens may migrate, so follow the [native upgrade procedure](docs/user-guide.md#native-beads-store-behavior) before upgrading `bd`. The patch has deterministic and packaged regression checks; the bounded native host evidence remains the recorded 2.2.0 baseline, not a new live qualification campaign.

### Upgrading to 2.2.0

Upgrade OpenCode before changing the plugin pin: 2.2.0 requires `>=2.3.0 <2.4`. Then replace the existing plugin entry, not add a second one, and check `/oc-beads:diagnostics`. Existing exact 1.x and beta pins remain available; installations are not upgraded automatically. Staying on OpenCode 2.1? Keep the exact `1.1.0-beta.5` pin, which retains its `>=2.1.1 <2.2` range. Other migration notes are in the [user guide](docs/user-guide.md#upgrading).

For OpenCode 2.2, keep the released exact `2.1.0` plugin pin; it retains `>=2.2.6 <2.3` support. Version 2.2.0 changes the host range while retaining existing options. To add the optional `beads-task-agent-terra` profile, enable `terra: true` in the object form. It uses `openai/gpt-6.1-terra#medium`; the default agent still inherits its model, Luna Max remains available, and both optional profiles can coexist. Enabling a profile does not authorize work or change the parent route.

## First use

In an initialized project:

```text
/oc-beads:diagnostics
/oc-beads:ready
```

Diagnostics confirms what loaded and which capabilities this request actually has. `ready` lists actionable work; listing alone never claims anything. Then ask in plain language, for example:

```text
Claim bd-a1b2 and work it to its acceptance criteria. Checkpoint what you learn.
```

The agent claims the issue atomically and appends checkpoints under the actual session-and-agent actor. It validates against acceptance, then stops with that item instead of picking up other work. Each typed operation is checked against your OpenCode permission rules. To delegate, ask the agent to hand the issue to `beads-task-agent`.

## Known limitations

- **Workflow guidance after a model switch.** This is an unresolved deficiency. After native conversation compaction on model A, switching to model B that cannot replay A's native context can make earlier workflow instruction snapshots and captured diagnostics unavailable. The plugin reports that guidance as unavailable and continues with the ordinary request; it does not reconstruct it. The limitation affects prompt guidance only: it does not change or repair the Beads issue database or its stored data. It is tracked upstream as [upstream issue #57424](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/issues/57424) and locally as `opencode-beads-o66`.
- **Rejecting a permission is not Stop.** If you reject one nested operation, it does not run and is not retried. However, that does not promise to end the rest of the composition, because each later operation gets its own permission check. Use explicit Stop/Cancel to stop the composition.
- **Bounded evidence.** Bounded qualification covers exact OpenCode 2.3.0 and a genuine OpenAI workflow, with the deferred cases described above. It is not a model-reliability, token-saving, cross-provider checkpoint or multi-hour claim.

# ADR-0001: Keep exact CLI syntax dynamic

## Status

Accepted for this guidance corpus.

## Context

The upstream Beads skill and its resources have useful decision guidance, but
they are not a generated reference for every installed `bd` release. Copying
flags and command forms throughout prose lets examples age independently of the
CLI. A successful `bd prime` or command exit is also not proof that a particular
record was found, a memory was returned, or a write was acknowledged.

## Decision

- Keep cognitive and workflow guidance in `SKILL.md` and its on-demand resources.
- Use `bd prime` for current workflow context and `bd '<command>' --help` for
  exact syntax. Do not duplicate a broad CLI reference here.
- Respect an explicit context or permission hold. A manual prime is
  not a fallback around a hold.
- Keep examples limited to supported CLI forms verified against the installed
  help. When an operation is unavailable, say what supported path or limitation
  applies instead of inventing a flag or tool.
- Treat host registration, package inclusion, installed resource access, and
  behavioral qualification as separate evidence. The presence of these source
  assets does not establish those outcomes.

## Consequences

This keeps the startup guidance short and moves depth to linked resources. CLI
help can still be incomplete or ambiguous, so examples and compatibility claims
need review against their relevant Beads release. No claim that drift is
impossible is made. Advanced features remain opt-in and do not enable automation,
store initialization, synchronization, or permission changes by themselves.

# Asynchronous gates

> Adapted from [Beads marketplace-main `ASYNC_GATES.md`](https://github.com/gastownhall/beads/blob/4a67d0d0288c1b4ee23e17fc896f47616931ba2d/plugins/beads/skills/beads/resources/ASYNC_GATES.md).

An async gate models a wait condition that blocks a later step. It does not do
the work, grant permission, or make a human decision. Use one only when an
authorized workflow needs a durable wait relationship; ordinary blockers can
remain issue dependencies.

## Gate kinds

The pinned guidance distinguishes a human decision from a condition that can
be checked:

| Kind | Successful condition | Failure or timeout behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `human` | Explicit human decision, recorded by manual resolution. | A `--timeout` can be stored as metadata but is not enforced by `bd gate check`; silence is not consent. |
| `timer` | The timeout has elapsed when an authorized executor runs `bd gate check --type=timer --actor='<executor-actor>' --sandbox --json`. | Otherwise it remains pending. |
| `gh:run` | Run is completed with success (the pinned guidance also treats skipped as resolved). | Completed failure or cancellation escalates; the gate remains open for a decision. |
| `gh:pr` | Pull request is merged. | Closed without merge escalates; the gate remains open for a decision. |
| `bead` | The referenced issue is closed, when supported by the installed create path. | An open target remains pending. |

The installed `bd gate check --help` confirms timer evaluation and GitHub
success/failure conditions. The pinned source says a human gate's stored timeout
is not enforced by `check`. The installed `bd gate create --help` lists human,
timer, `gh:run`, and `gh:pr`; it does not list `bead` as a create type. Check
current help before relying on a gate type; this guidance does not qualify host
behavior.

## Inspect and resolve deliberately

Use `bd gate --help` and `bd gate '<subcommand>' --help` for current syntax. The
installed help supports this deliberate human-decision flow:

```sh
# An authorized executor creates the wait condition.
bd gate create --type=human --blocks='<issue-id>' \
  --reason="Needs owner review" --actor='<executor-actor>' --sandbox --json
bd gate list --json
bd gate show '<gate-id>'

# The actual human runs this command only after making the decision.
bd gate resolve '<gate-id>' --reason="Reviewed; decision recorded" \
  --actor='<actual-human-actor>' --sandbox --json
```

Read both the gate and blocked issue before changing either. An agent must never
supply a human actor or resolve a human gate on the human's behalf. Never infer
consent from silence. A failed CI run or unmerged closed pull request is a failure
to investigate, not a successful gate. If an authorized executor runs a check, keep its actor explicit and
inspect the resulting state before continuing.

Do not create gates automatically for every handoff, approval, test, or issue.
Do not add polling, watchers, or approval automation as a side effect of reading
this resource. Gates and issue dependencies are distinct: use a gate for a
documented async condition, and an issue dependency for work ordering.

## Stop conditions

Stop if the gate cannot be read, its referenced event cannot be verified, a
human decision is required, or the current CLI lacks the required gate action.
Report the gate ID, observed state, evidence, and the decision needed. Never
route around a permission denial by calling a different interface.

# Boundaries: durable tracking and short-lived work

> Adapted from [Beads marketplace-main `BOUNDARIES.md`](https://github.com/gastownhall/beads/blob/4a67d0d0288c1b4ee23e17fc896f47616931ba2d/plugins/beads/skills/beads/resources/BOUNDARIES.md).

Use Beads for work whose ownership, dependencies, blocker, history, or next
session matters to the project. Keep a short linear breakdown in the current
conversation when it is only an execution aid and no repository rule requires a
durable issue. Do not make a second Markdown task list the durable project record.

## Choose the right record

| Situation | Record | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Short, linear steps that will finish in this session | Conversation checklist, if useful | Keeps execution visible without creating durable issue noise. |
| Work needs an owner, blocker, dependency, acceptance, or later resume | Existing or authorized Bead | Preserves execution history and handoff context. |
| Validated learning is likely to help on future issues | Relevant Beads memory | Reusable knowledge is separate from a task's attempts. |
| Intended behavior and acceptance contract | Project's specification system (for example OpenSpec, when used) | Keeps the project specification authoritative. |
| Detailed rationale, source evidence, or qualification result | Project documentation | Gives durable evidence a stable home. |
| Temporary command output | Current session; summarize only if it changes a decision | Avoids storing noise. |
| Host explicitly exposes experimental todo support and the user/project opts in | Host-owned transient checklist | Optional convenience only; it is not installed or enabled here. |

OpenCode 2.1 experimental todo support is opt-in and host-owned. Do not require
it, turn it on, or assume Claude's `TodoWrite` exists in every host. If no
session checklist is available, keep a brief checklist in the conversation or
use an authorized Bead when the work is durable.

Do not create a new Bead for every command, transient retry, small nit, or
document. Create or update a record when the work is genuinely durable and you
have authority to do so. Existing assignment and project policy take priority
over any general heuristic here.

Ask: “Could I resume this after two weeks away?” If the answer needs context
that would otherwise be lost, preserve it in the appropriate authorized record.

## Transition when the work grows

It is reasonable to begin with a transient checklist for “update the retry
message and run its focused test.” If the test uncovers an independent data-loss
case, a prerequisite, or work that must continue next session, stop treating the
checklist as the durable record. If authorized, create or update the appropriate
Bead with the attempted fix, test evidence, discovered blocker, acceptance, and
next step; link new work to its source where useful. Keep the checklist only for
the remaining steps in this session. Without authority to create or change a
Bead, preserve the discovery in the assigned record if permitted, then report
and stop at the scope boundary.

## Preserve the authority boundary

A ready issue is available work, not permission. A single-item assignment ends
after that item; continue only inside an explicitly authorized batch or goal.
Finding related work does not authorize acting on it. Link or report discoveries
only within the authority already granted.

For a tracked item, preserve its execution identity and history. Claim
atomically when authorized, use an explicit actor on writes, and append material
progress; a deliberate current-state handoff may replace working notes while
preserving relevant learning. A task record does not own the
Beads database or authorize sync, setup, permission changes, or Git operations.

# Molecule and wisp patterns

> Adapted from [Beads marketplace-main `CHEMISTRY_PATTERNS.md`](https://github.com/gastownhall/beads/blob/4a67d0d0288c1b4ee23e17fc896f47616931ba2d/plugins/beads/skills/beads/resources/CHEMISTRY_PATTERNS.md).

Molecules and wisps are advanced ways to organize repeated or temporary work.
They are optional. A normal issue and its dependencies are usually enough for
one task. Do not introduce a molecule workflow simply because it is available.

## Choose by phase and lifetime

| Need | Record | Lifetime |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One-off owned work with no reusable workflow | Normal issue and dependencies | Durable issue history. |
| Repeated multi-step work whose children and audit trail should persist | Formula/proto instantiated as a persistent molecule | Reusable source, then durable execution records. |
| Authorized short-lived research, review, triage, or operations with low audit value | Wisp from an existing formula/proto | Ephemeral; useful findings must be promoted before cleanup. |

Treat formulas/protos as reusable workflow sources, molecules as instantiated
work, and wisps as the temporary phase. Do not use a wisp when the full trail
must persist or assume that a formula will stay inside the exact assignment.

Before using a formula, inspect the available formula and its steps. Decide what
evidence should survive and who owns each child. Do not let a template silently
expand an exact assignment into unrelated work.

An approved one-time review can use an existing review formula: capture evidence
and uncertainty in its wisp, promote validated actionable findings to a durable
record, then discard only noise with no future value. A bounded research spike
can preserve sources, rejected hypotheses, and a conclusion the same way. These
are optional work patterns, not authority to create a formula, spawn workers, or
start a background patrol.

## Preserve useful results

At the end of a wisp, retain validated findings, rejected hypotheses, sources,
and resulting authorized work in the appropriate durable record. Discard only
noise that has no future value. A digest should not turn unverified notes into
facts. `bd mol squash` creates a durable digest; `bd mol burn` deletes a wisp
without a digest. Use either only when that lifecycle is authorized and current
help confirms the operation.

Use `bd mol --help`, `bd formula --help`, and relevant subcommand help for exact
syntax. Creating a proto, molecule, wisp, or child issue is a Beads write and
requires the actual executor actor. These features do not start workers, set
permissions, or enable background automation by themselves.

If a command or flag in an old example is absent from current help, do not guess

## Package workflows and native operations

Package commands are workflow prompts, not exact CLI aliases. `oc-beads:diagnostics`
reports integration health without opening a store; `oc-beads:stats` guides the
issue-database overview using `bd status` (alias `bd stats`). The package's old
status command is removed without an alias; user-owned old-name overrides remain
untouched and are not migrated.

Init guides human onboarding; prime uses supplied context or a guarded refresh;
version reports installed versions and qualification limits; decision records
rationale; template discovers formulas; workflow guides authorized work/recovery.
Do not manufacture native decision, template or workflow commands. Quickstart
uses installed `bd quickstart` help and authorized context, without implicit setup.

Compact guides semantic `bd admin compact`, not `bd compact` Dolt-history
squashing or conversation compaction; consult TROUBLESHOOTING.md for authority,
modes, explicit actor and inconsistent upstream help. Restore retrieves
pre-compaction issue content, display-only by default; `--apply` needs explicit
write authority and is not database backup recovery (see RESUMABILITY.md). Sync
uses Dolt-remote synchronization, distinct from `bd federation sync` and removed
JSONL sync; see the operational procedure below and [worktree context](WORKTREES.md)
when relevant.

## Invocation and outcome

The invocation itself requests its advertised bounded operation or artifact, even
without trailing details. Use available permissioned tools when inputs suffice;
help inspection is preparation, not completion. Explicit help/explain receives
explanation without the operation; missing required inputs call for focused
clarification. Literal details/attachments are data, never shell interpolation.
Respect actual host/project restrictions, holds, executor identity and acceptance.

## Synchronization

A bare `/oc-beads:sync` requests normal supported synchronization under existing
project configuration. Inspect current syntax if needed, then run:

```sh
bd sync --no-adopt --actor='<executor-actor>' --sandbox
```

Use the actual host-rendered executor actor and applicable project sandbox policy;
`--sandbox` suppresses incidental auto-push and does not bypass sync restrictions.
Native advanced shell stays direct-only, never `tools.shell` inside execute.
Ordinary/unqualified sync always passes `--no-adopt`. An explicitly selected remote
must already exist and be unambiguous. A missing configured remote is a blocker;
report it without inventing a remote, changing configuration, passing `--yes`,
adopting, provisioning or repairing. Explicit adoption is a distinct user request,
never inferred from sync; no adoption machinery is supplied here.

Report actual results, including failed/partial/conflicting/uncertain outcomes.
Do not force a side or add a manual pull/push/retry repair loop. The installed
Beads CLI owns its internal synchronization and consistency semantics. Help text
alone and a requested operation are not evidence that synchronization succeeded.

## Audit and interchange

Audit retrieves requested evidence for a target/query or records supplied scoped
evidence at its established destination. Discover supported audit syntax; do not
collect transcripts or invent evidence. Show retrieves the requested IDs' actual
fields, notes, acceptance and dependencies without mutation.

Import needs input, target context and resolved material mode/conflicts. Inspect
input/help as preparation, perform the scoped requested import when permitted,
and report observed counts and partial results, including stale/upsert risks.
Never initialize, restore or repair implicitly. Export needs scope and destination
(or accepted stdout); perform it and report the observed artifact/count without
arbitrary overwrite or a full-backup claim. See [troubleshooting](TROUBLESHOOTING.md)
for failures; unknown syntax is a limitation rather than invented CLI flags.

## Onboarding and discovery

Init and quickstart deliver a usable human-directed guide with current installed
help, relevant project context and concrete next steps/side effects. They do not
initialize a store automatically. Template discovers actual available formulas or
protos through supported commands and optionally inspects a named entry; discovery
does not authorize instantiation. Report actual entries or unavailability.
Decision persists supplied rationale/alternatives in the established project-owned
destination; clarify only if it cannot be resolved, and do not invent a native
command or automatically create a new issue/spec/document. Bare workflow delivers
a procedure; task execution needs an already authorized assignment or batch.

# Beads in native code mode

Use the actual request capability block. When the beads namespace is registered
and execute is visible, use native `search({namespace: "beads"})` to discover
current signatures. Catalog discovery and each operation's permissions determine
what is callable; execute visibility alone does not establish leaf availability.
Do not copy a signature catalog from prose or invent tools. When a host exposes
namespaced Beads leaves directly, use only those actually visible leaves and
their current signatures; each operation still has its own permission check.
Permissioned direct shell is independently available only when shown, authorized
and no guard hold applies. Do not retry a rejected operation through another
surface; preserve explicit Stop/Cancel. Native shell is **direct-only**: never
call `tools.shell` inside execute. Repository editing, tests and Git run in
separate direct shell turns.

## Read, choose, then act

Start with bounded discovery and inspect scope and `complete`. `true` refers to
that query, `false` means truncated or partial, and `null` means completeness is
unknown. Ready, list, search and blocked have different supported filters;
unsupported combinations are rejected. Blocked and edge reads can return unknown
completeness. Unknown or failed edges never prove that work is unblocked.

Get chosen IDs together (at most 25); the adapter performs sequential single-ID
reads. Inspect per-ID failures and `complete`; an all-failed get is failed, not
missing. There is no snapshot-consistency or transaction promise. For independent
reads, use small bounded fan-out (for example at most eight candidates with
`Promise.allSettled`), retain rejected/failed outcomes as unknowns, and return a
projection of relevant fields. Return memory keys first, then recall selected
keys. A found empty memory differs from a missing key; memories retains a
key-to-value map, including a successful empty map.

Selecting a candidate does not authorize claiming it. Read scope, prior attempts,
acceptance and dependencies before acting. Await an authorized claim and stop
dependent work unless it acknowledges the actual executor as assignee in
`in_progress`. A claim never hides a second readback prompt; use get explicitly
when needed. `not-claimed` requires evidenced non-claim, and `uncertain` requires
current-state inspection before considering another write.

## Ordered writes and honest outcomes

Await dependent writes in order; inspect each result before the next call. Do not
parallelize claim, note, update, close or dependent creates. Each invocation has
its own canonical permission resources and `save: []`: an "always" response may
apply to that call only, so ask may prompt again. Saved shell grants remain
subject to denies. Orchestrator authority does not bypass host permission prompts.
Do not catch a rejected operation and continue its dependent writes. Plain
permission decline on OpenCode 2.1.1 may still permit later independently
permissioned work or model steps; it does not promise whole-program termination.
Explicit Stop/Cancel is distinct and its installed qualification remains separate.

Use note for append checkpoints. Selected-field update excludes ownership changes
and closure. Close needs caller-authorized acceptance evidence; it is never an
automatic workflow step. Create generates an ID and does not automatically assign
an executor. An uncertain create retains its identifying query/title: search and
read back before considering a manual retry, to avoid duplicates.

Every typed write returns the host-derived actor. Use that same rendered actor
for direct shell writes, claims and heartbeats with command-scoped `--actor` or
`BEADS_ACTOR`, and `--sandbox` to suppress automatic Dolt push. No global actor
configuration, model-controlled actor argument or human Git fallback. A child
uses its own actual session/agent actor and claims only authorized work; parent
review does not transfer assignment. Audit author (`created_by`), account owner
(`owner`) and executor (`assignee`) are separate observations; missing fields
remain unknown. Attribution is not permission or authentication.

Only authoritative CLI evidence acknowledges a write. Started interrupted,
timed-out or malformed writes may have landed: retain target, actor and original
diagnostic, then inspect durable state under fresh authorization. Do not blindly
retry, force, commit or synchronize. A landed but uncommitted memory retains
`commit_error`/`commit_indeterminate`; it is not committed durability. Fulfilled
Promises, outer execute completion and compaction summaries do not establish
successful persistence. Write inputs remain in host trace metadata.

Full prime remains the canonical workflow reference. Meaningful checkpoints
carry attempts, measured outcomes, rationale, blockers and next action. Important
recovery, external changes and actual child reports require fresh relevant state;
acknowledged writes do not require a generic redundant read of their own result.
Preserve distinct repository/user authority, guard holds and exact scope. Missing
capability or failed context is reported honestly, without manual-prime bypass,
implicit sync, automatic retries or a replacement workflow manager.

# Dependency types and direction

> Adapted from [Beads marketplace-main `DEPENDENCIES.md`](https://github.com/gastownhall/beads/blob/4a67d0d0288c1b4ee23e17fc896f47616931ba2d/plugins/beads/skills/beads/resources/DEPENDENCIES.md).

Beads dependencies describe relationships between issues. Confirm direction
before writing: in the current `bd create` help, a bare ID, `'depends-on:<id>'`, or
`'blocked-by:<id>'` makes the new issue depend on that ID; `'blocks:<id>'` reverses
that direction. For existing issues, the installed `bd dep add --help` confirms
the dependent comes first and the prerequisite second (default type: `blocks`).

## Choose a relationship by meaning

| Question | Relationship | Effect to preserve |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Can B start before A is complete? | `blocks` (A blocks B) | Hard ordering constraint; the dependent waits. |
| Is B part of A's planned work? | `parent-child` (A parent, B child) | Decomposition and ownership; not an ordering edge. |
| Did work on A uncover B? | `discovered-from` (B from A) | Discovery provenance; not permission to start B. |
| Are A and B connected but independently actionable? | `related` | Informational association, not a blocker. |

For a new dependent issue, current `bd create --help` says that
`--deps='depends-on:<prerequisite-id>'` means **this new issue depends on that
prerequisite**. For example, an API task can depend on a schema task like this:

```sh
bd create "Implement API" --type=task \
  --parent='<epic-id>' \
  --deps='depends-on:<schema-task-id>' \
  --actor='<executor-actor>' --sandbox --json
```

The command above makes the API task a child of an epic while also adding a
separate hard blocker on schema setup. Read back both edges: hierarchy answers
“what work belongs here?”; a blocker answers “what must finish first?”. Add a
hard block only when a real prerequisite exists.

### Add and check existing-issue edges

X needs Y means X depends on Y: dependent first, prerequisite second.

```sh
bd dep add '<dependent-id>' '<prerequisite-id>' --actor='<executor-actor>' --sandbox --json
bd blocked --json
bd dep list '<dependent-id>' --json
```

Phase trap: “Phase 1 before Phase 2” means Phase 2 needs Phase 1.
Wrong: `bd dep add '<phase-1-id>' '<phase-2-id>' --actor='<executor-actor>' --sandbox --json` would block Phase 1.
Right: `bd dep add '<phase-2-id>' '<phase-1-id>' --actor='<executor-actor>' --sandbox --json` blocks Phase 2 on Phase 1.
Readback: `bd blocked` should show the dependent waiting while its prerequisite
is open; `bd dep list` defaults to dependencies (down), so it should list that
prerequisite, never the dependent's later work. These reads do not authorize work.

### Diamond and parallel merge

```text
                  setup
                 /     \
            API work   UI work
                 \     /
                 integration tests

setup blocks API work and UI work; each implementation blocks the merge tests.
The two implementations can proceed in parallel after setup.
```

`related` is useful for an optional improvement that should remain independently
ready. A discovery cascade is different: B may be discovered from A, and C from
B, preserving how the questions emerged. `discovered-from` does not make that
cascade required work, grant authority, or create a hard blocker.

Use the narrowest accurate relation. Do not use a hard blocker for a preference,
shared topic, or unverified assumption. Avoid cycles and redundant edges. Before
adding or changing an edge, inspect both issues and verify which one depends on
which. Afterward, read the graph back when the relationship affects readiness.

Dependency direction is especially easy to reverse when creating a child or
recording discovery. The current CLI help is authoritative for syntax; this page
preserves relationship meaning, not every command form. Agent-authored graph
writes require an explicit executor actor. A ready result is only a scheduling
view: it does not override assignment, task scope, or authorization. The
installed CLI describes hard blockers as affecting readiness; inspect the graph
after a meaningful edit rather than inferring it from the prose alone.

# Integrating Beads with project workflow

> Adapted from [Beads marketplace-main `INTEGRATION_PATTERNS.md`](https://github.com/gastownhall/beads/blob/4a67d0d0288c1b4ee23e17fc896f47616931ba2d/plugins/beads/skills/beads/resources/INTEGRATION_PATTERNS.md).

Use Beads to preserve execution state, not to replace every other source of
intent or evidence. A useful division is:

| Need | Source of truth |
| --- | --- |
| Intended behavior, requirements, and acceptance contract | Project's specification system (for example OpenSpec, when used) |
| Detailed rationale, measurements, source references, and qualification evidence | Project documentation |
| Execution ownership, dependencies, blockers, progress notes, and status | Beads |
| Short checklist for today's already-authorized steps | Current session or optional host-owned todo, if available |

Link those records when the relationship helps a future reader. Do not duplicate
an entire design or test log in Beads; append a concise checkpoint with the
result, why it matters, and where the detailed evidence lives.

## Worked linkage: plan, review, then execute

This is a project-policy example, not a universal Beads requirement. Use the
project's chosen planning and review rules; the pattern below is optional where
no such policy exists.

For example, an OpenSpec change, in a project that uses it, can own the behavior
and acceptance criteria for a new export option. Put detailed trade-offs and test
evidence in a linked project document. A quick planning draft needs no separate Bead. For substantial
multi-session or delegated planning, create one bounded planning Bead, distinct
from the implementation epic, and reference the OpenSpec change and evidence
document there.

When review is independently owned and substantive, use one bounded review
Bead linked to the planning work and the exact candidate revision. Record the
reviewer's actual actor/session, verdict, findings, and evidence. Reuse that
same review Bead for correction and recheck cycles; do not create a ticket per
document, retry, or transient nit. Implementation issues track the authorized
execution work. The chosen specification system and docs remain the spec/evidence
sources, not duplicate task trackers; planning or review completion does not
authorize implementation or prove parent acceptance. A ready Bead is not dispatch authority.

## Milestones and recovery

Read existing issue notes and relevant project memory before choosing a next
step. At a material milestone, append attempted work, result, rationale, changed
decision, blocker, and next action. Use the explicit executor actor. If the
operation does not materially change the work context, no redundant write is
needed.

```sh
bd update '<execution-id>' \
  --append-notes="Tried X; observed Y in tests/export.test.ts; chose Z because …; blocker …; next …" \
  --actor='<executor-actor>' --sandbox --json
```

For delegation, send the worker the exact authorized scope and its actual actor.
Ask for the attempt, outcome, evidence, rationale, blocker, next step, and any
durable record references. The parent reconciles the return against the original
intent and acceptance before continuing or closing. Delegation is discretionary;
do not route work based on a command count.

OpenCode 2.1 experimental todo support remains opt-in and host-owned. Use it only
when that host feature is actually available and the user/project chooses it;
do not enable it or present it as a universal `TodoWrite` tool. It can hold a
temporary execution checklist, not replace the project's specification system,
project evidence, or Beads.

## Keep durable and transient information distinct

Task-specific findings stay with the task. Reusable memory is reserved for
validated knowledge likely to apply elsewhere. Transient shell output and
temporary execution checklists stay local unless they change a decision or must
survive resumption. Existing user and repository instructions remain in force;
an integration does not grant new authority to create issues, mutate other
records, or broaden a task.

# Creating useful issues

> Adapted from Beads [`ISSUE_CREATION.md`](https://github.com/gastownhall/beads/blob/5ac194105c138ca799bc2f6534c8f92712d8d782/plugins/beads/skills/beads/resources/ISSUE_CREATION.md) at `5ac194105c138ca799bc2f6534c8f92712d8d782`; see [third-party notices](../THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md).

Create a durable issue when work needs its own assignment, dependencies,
multi-session history, or acceptance record, and only when the existing authority
allows creation. Do not create one for every retry, note, or discovered idea.
Discovery may be reported without being worked; a `discovered-from` edge does
not authorize the new issue.

## Write for the next executor

- **Title:** a specific outcome or problem.
- **Description:** why the work exists, relevant context, and boundaries.
- **Design:** the intended approach and important constraints.
- **Acceptance:** observable conditions that define completion.
- **Notes:** evolving progress, incremental checkpoints and deliberate current-state handoffs.

Do not treat a proposed approach as an acceptance test. Avoid secrets, copied
logs, vague “investigate” titles without a question, and unsupported promises.
Leave new work unassigned unless an assignment is intentional. If a human owns
the work, assign that person deliberately; an agent actor is not proof of
permission.

Keep design and acceptance distinct: design records a candidate approach and
trade-offs that may change; acceptance states a testable outcome that remains
true if the implementation changes. For example, “reuse the current parser if
it handles quoted fields” is design; “quoted commas and quotes round-trip in the
export” is acceptance. Put the former in `--design` and the latter in
`--acceptance`.

Current syntax comes from `bd create --help`. A write must use the actual
executor actor, for example:

```sh
bd create "Clarify retry behavior" --type=task --priority=2 \
  --description="Record the user-visible issue and affected path." \
  --design="Trace the current behavior and document the supported correction." \
  --acceptance="The behavior and validation evidence are recorded." \
  --actor='<executor-actor>' --sandbox --json
```

Before creating linked work, inspect the parent and verify dependency direction.
Keep planning and implementation ownership distinct when the project assigns
them to different people.

## Design vs Acceptance Criteria (Critical Distinction) {#design-vs-acceptance}

Common mistake: Putting implementation details in acceptance criteria. Here's the difference:

### DESIGN field (HOW to build it):
- "Use two-phase batchUpdate approach: insert text first, then apply formatting"
- "Parse with regex to find * and _ markers"
- "Use JWT tokens with 1-hour expiry"
- Trade-offs: "Chose batchUpdate over streaming API for atomicity"

### ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA (WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE):
- "Bold and italic markdown formatting renders correctly in the Doc"
- "Solution accepts markdown input and creates Doc with specified title"
- "Returns doc_id and webViewLink to caller"
- "User tokens persist across sessions and refresh automatically"

### Why this matters:
- Design can change during implementation (e.g., use library instead of regex)
- Acceptance criteria should remain stable across sessions
- Criteria should be **outcome-focused** ("what must be true?") not **step-focused** ("do these steps")
- Each criterion should be **verifiable** - you can definitively say yes/no

### The pitfall

Writing criteria like "- [ ] Use batchUpdate approach" locks you into one implementation.

Better: "- [ ] Formatting is applied atomically (all at once or not at all)" - allows flexible implementation.

### Test yourself

If you rewrote the solution using a different approach, would the acceptance criteria still apply? If not, they're design notes, not criteria.

### Example of correct structure

✅ **Design field:**
```
Two-phase Docs API approach:
1. Parse markdown to positions
2. Create doc + insert text in one call
3. Apply formatting in second call
Rationale: Atomic operations, easier to debug formatting separately
```

✅ **Acceptance criteria:**
```
- [ ] Markdown formatting renders in Doc (bold, italic, headings)
- [ ] Lists preserve order and nesting
- [ ] Links are clickable
- [ ] Large documents (>50KB) process without timeout
```

❌ **Wrong (design masquerading as criteria):**
```
- [ ] Use two-phase batchUpdate approach
- [ ] Apply formatting in second batchUpdate call
```

# Molecules, formulas, and wisps

> Adapted from [Beads marketplace-main `MOLECULES.md`](https://github.com/gastownhall/beads/blob/4a67d0d0288c1b4ee23e17fc896f47616931ba2d/plugins/beads/skills/beads/resources/MOLECULES.md).

The current CLI describes formulas as workflow sources, protos as reusable
templates, molecules as instantiated work, and wisps as ephemeral workflows.
Use these only when their lifecycle solves a real project need; a normal issue
graph is clearer for one-off work.

## Decide before instantiating

| Question | Choose |
| --- | --- |
| Is this one-off work with a clear owner and no template need? | A normal issue graph. |
| Must each step and its audit history remain durable? | Persistent molecule with durable audit history from an inspected formula/proto. |
| Is the work short-lived and low-audit, with an agreed way to preserve findings? | Wisp, only with explicit lifecycle authority. |
| Is the workflow repeatable and already validated? | Consider distilling a formula after preserving its evidence and lessons. |

Inspect the formula's gates, dependencies, variables, and children before
creating work. Confirm that every step fits the authorized scope. Keep generated
children aligned with the intended parent acceptance; closed children do not
prove the parent outcome.

## Example: approved review wisp

When a bounded review is authorized as temporary and an existing review proto
fits the scope, create the wisp, inspect its instantiated steps, and retain only
validated findings:

```sh
bd mol wisp create '<review-proto-id>' --var 'candidate=<revision>' \
  --actor='<executor-actor>' --sandbox --json
bd mol show '<wisp-id>'
```

If the review produced reusable evidence or actionable findings, summarize and
promote the result to a durable digest:

```sh
bd mol squash '<wisp-id>' \
  --summary="Candidate <revision>: verified findings and evidence references" \
  --actor='<executor-actor>' --sandbox --json
```

If the wisp contains only noise with no future value, burn it only when that
deletion is explicitly authorized; this leaves no digest:

```sh
bd mol burn '<wisp-id>' --actor='<executor-actor>' --sandbox --json
```

These verbs and phase effects are confirmed by installed subcommand help. A
wisp is ephemeral and not synced via Git; do not use it as the only home for
required acceptance evidence. A digest is a summary, not proof that findings
were independently validated or that a parent issue is accepted.

Distilling a formula is useful only after a workflow has proved repeatable.
Retain validation and lessons in the reusable template, not accidental details
from one run. Bonding workflows can create large graphs; inspect the result and
ownership before proceeding. Do not pour, bond, squash, burn, or distill as
automatic setup or background orchestration.

Use `bd formula --help` and `bd mol --help`, then each relevant subcommand's
help, for current syntax. These are state changes; keep the actual executor
actor explicit.

# Common execution patterns

> Adapted from [Beads marketplace-main `PATTERNS.md`](https://github.com/gastownhall/beads/blob/4a67d0d0288c1b4ee23e17fc896f47616931ba2d/plugins/beads/skills/beads/resources/PATTERNS.md).

## Start with the actual request

Read the assigned issue, parent decisions, relevant dependencies, and current
notes. Distinguish the requested result from a suggested implementation. A
ready issue or an open side quest does not itself authorize work.

## Record a side discovery without expanding scope

When a new concern appears, preserve enough evidence to explain it. If recording
it is authorized, create a concise issue and link its provenance. Continue only
if the current authorization explicitly includes it. Otherwise finish the
assigned work, report the discovery, and stop.

## Resume a multi-session task

Read the latest appended checkpoint and relevant reusable memory. Reconfirm the
state from the issue or current evidence instead of assuming the prior next step
still applies. Preserve rejected approaches so the next executor does not repeat
them.

For research or debugging, keep the hypothesis, the attempt, and the evidence
that changed the conclusion together. A rejected hypothesis is useful when its
failure is explained; an unexplained “tried X” is not. If the changed conclusion
creates separate durable work, record its source only when authorized. Discovery
does not by itself make that work a blocker or assign it to the current executor.

## Change status and close carefully

Use the installed CLI's valid transitions. Claim only the item you are
authorized to execute; keep the actual executor actor on claim, updates, and
heartbeats. Before closure, compare the deliverable with acceptance criteria and
record validation results. If a blocker or failed check remains, report it and
leave the state accurate. If someone else owns acceptance, return the evidence
instead of closing on their behalf.

There is no mandatory one-issue-per-session cadence. Keep each Bead's evidence
clear, while following an explicitly authorized multi-item batch where one was
granted. Use `bd '<command>' --help` for current syntax; do not use old MCP-only
examples or replace notes during ordinary checkpoints.

# Resumability and recovery

> Adapted from Beads [`RESUMABILITY.md`](https://github.com/gastownhall/beads/blob/5ac194105c138ca799bc2f6534c8f92712d8d782/plugins/beads/skills/beads/resources/RESUMABILITY.md) at `5ac194105c138ca799bc2f6534c8f92712d8d782`; see [third-party notices](../THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md).

A future executor needs the state of the work, not a transcript. At meaningful
transitions preserve:

1. what was attempted and why;
2. the observed result and evidence location;
3. the decision or hypothesis that changed;
4. what remains blocked or uncertain; and
5. one concrete next action within the assigned scope.

Append this checkpoint to the issue so earlier attempts remain visible. Do not
copy full logs, secrets, or unverified conclusions. An abrupt process stop can
prevent a final write, so checkpoint after important results instead of relying
on end-of-session cleanup.

## Example: make a thin checkpoint resumable

### Before checkpoint

```text
Tried the export change; the test still fails.
```

### After checkpoint

```text
Attempted: split export rows on commas.
Observed evidence: tests/export.test.ts, case quoted-comma still fails;
  fixture: tests/fixtures/quoted-comma.csv.
Rationale: commas inside quoted fields are data, so splitting cannot work.
Blocker: confirm whether the existing parser exposes a streaming API.
Next: inspect the parser contract, then add a regression test before changing it.
```

The second checkpoint carries the approach, observed evidence and its location,
the decision it supports, the remaining uncertainty, and one next action. Use a
small handoff shape when the example is too detailed:

### Minimal handoff template

```text
Task and scope:
Attempt and result (evidence/reference):
Decision and rationale:
Blocker or uncertainty:
Next authorized step:
```

Add a tested minimal command or code snippet only when the next executor needs
it to reproduce a hard-to-infer result or response shape. Mark what was actually
run and where. Otherwise link to the relevant test or document and summarize the
result. Do not paste raw logs, giant JSON dumps, credentials, or speculative
snippets; acceptance describes the observable outcome, while notes retain
implementation discoveries and rationale.

## Resume safely

For a cold start or after compaction, recover the assigned work rather than
selecting fresh work from `bd ready`:

```sh
bd list --status=in_progress --assignee='<executor-actor>' --json
bd show '<issue-id>' --long --json
```

Use your actual assignment actor for the assignee filter. If the assignment
already gives an exact issue ID, show that issue directly; an empty list is not
permission to claim another task. Read the latest appended checkpoint and earlier
notes for attempts, evidence, decisions, blockers, and the next authorized step.
Retrieve only relevant reusable memory, then verify current assignment, status,
dependencies, and time-sensitive evidence before acting. The issue notes explain
work on this item; memory carries validated learning beyond it. Neither should
override current user or repository instructions.

Treat missing context, failed retrieval, and deliberately withheld context as
different outcomes. An explicit authority or permission hold is not an invitation to run a
manual fallback. If a write timed out, read the issue before retrying; the first
write may have landed. Preserve uncertainty explicitly until it is resolved.

Use the current CLI syntax from `bd prime` and command help when authorized.

## Restore pre-compaction issue content

`oc-beads:restore` guides `bd restore` retrieval of pre-compaction issue content,
display-only by default. `--apply` requires explicit authority to write that
content back to the issue. This is not database backup recovery, Git history
restoration or general store repair. Inspect installed help and report missing
content or uncertainty honestly; conflicting compact/restore help does not
establish guaranteed recovery or reversibility.

# Troubleshooting and stop conditions

> Curated replacement for [Beads marketplace-main `TROUBLESHOOTING.md`](https://github.com/gastownhall/beads/blob/4a67d0d0288c1b4ee23e17fc896f47616931ba2d/plugins/beads/skills/beads/resources/TROUBLESHOOTING.md). Legacy repair examples are not carried forward where they imply setup, server changes, or automatic repair.

## Context is absent, failed, or withheld

First identify which state actually occurred. If no context was provided, retrieve
current CLI context only when permitted and no hold is active. If retrieval
failed, report the error and preserve the task's last known state. If a compatibility check or explicit
permission restriction withheld context, stop; do not run `bd prime`, a different
CLI surface, or another agent as a bypass.

## A command or flag is unknown

Use `bd --help` and `bd '<command>' --help` to inspect the installed CLI. Do not
guess a flag from an old example, invoke a similarly named command, or assume an
MCP interface. If a workflow depends on an unavailable command, explain the
limitation and use a documented replacement only when it preserves the needed
semantics. The specialized `bd agent` and `bd slot` commands are absent from the
inspected CLI; see [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md).

## Compact operation and authority

`oc-beads:compact` guides semantic issue compaction with `bd admin compact`.
`bd compact` squashes Dolt history and is a different operation; neither means
conversation compaction. A bare invocation delivers a useful semantic guide or
analysis artifact. A sufficiently specified semantic apply request supplies its
bounded authority and does not need another generic approval. Clarify missing
scope, targets or consequential choices; preserve actual host/project restrictions
and inspect applicable installed help before action.

Prefer the agent-driven analyze/apply path. `--auto` sends issue content to an
external AI provider; `--dolt` performs storage garbage collection rather than
semantic summarization. These modes each require separate explicit authority;
ordinary compact approval selects neither. Always supply explicit `--actor`
for admin compact, which has its own local default of `agent`; do not inherit
that default or the human Git identity.

In the inspected Beads 1.3.1 help, admin compact's Usage/flags identify the semantic
operation but its examples still say `bd compact`. Its discard wording also
conflicts with restore's snapshot description. Do not copy those stale examples
or promise reversibility from that conflicting help. Report the uncertainty and
use applicable help and explicit authority for a future actual request. Do not
execute administration to validate this prose or repair upstream behavior.

## Store, migration, or routing problem

If the CLI reports no store, an outdated schema, an unexpected location, or a
redirect, do not initialize, migrate, reroute, repair, or synchronize it
automatically. Preserve the diagnostic and ask the authorized owner to choose a
supported recovery. The plugin's context guard is not permission to bypass the
same restriction through a shell command.

## Permission denial or external access prompt

Respect the decision. Do not switch to another tool, path, or identity to obtain
the same denied result. If a referenced guidance file is unreachable, state that
and continue only if the remaining task can be done safely and accurately.

## Empty result, failed read, or uncertain write

An empty successful query differs from an error. Report the actual result, not
the exit code alone. After a timeout or interrupted write, inspect the issue or
memory before retrying; the write may have landed. Do not blindly repeat a
create, claim, remember, or close operation.

## Lost claim or blocked task

Read the current assignee, status, and lease before continuing. If another actor
owns it or the claim was reclaimed, stop writes and coordinate a deliberate
handoff. Never force-reassign yourself or fall back to the human Git identity.
Record unresolved acceptance, missing evidence, and the next authorized action
in the handoff.

## Deletion and identifier migration

A sufficiently specified deletion invocation requests that bounded deletion.
Inspect target/effects and clarify unresolved destructive impact, then perform
only the requested deletion when policy and permissions permit. Do not replace
closure with deletion or silently expand cascades.

Bare rename-prefix delivers the advertised migration/reference-impact explanation.
A concrete migration requires a desired prefix and project scope; a fully scoped
migration request supplies its bounded authority without another generic approval.
Do not infer a prefix, migration or collateral rewrites. Real restrictions and
missing inputs still block; the invocation never bypasses permission or a hold.

# Workflows and checkpoints

> Adapted from Beads [`WORKFLOWS.md`](https://github.com/gastownhall/beads/blob/5ac194105c138ca799bc2f6534c8f92712d8d782/plugins/beads/skills/beads/resources/WORKFLOWS.md) at `5ac194105c138ca799bc2f6534c8f92712d8d782`; see [third-party notices](../THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md).

## Begin with the current context

Use current Beads context if it was supplied. Read the target issue, dependencies,
existing notes, and relevant memory before choosing an action. Confirm the exact
assignment and authority. Do not treat `ready` output as an assignment or
permission to work every listed item.

For an authorized task, claim it atomically with the actual executor actor. Keep
that actor on all subsequent writes and heartbeats. Direct execution is fine for
small tasks; use delegation where it improves the work, carrying a bounded scope
and the real delegate actor. Do not impose a one-item-per-invocation loop or
delegate by command count.

## Checkpoint at useful transitions

Append when a failed approach changes the next step, a finding is validated, a
decision changes, work becomes blocked, an actual child report arrives, or a session may stop.
Include the attempt, result, why it matters, evidence, blocker, and next action.
Use `--append-notes`, for example:

```sh
bd update '<id>' --append-notes="Validated …; evidence …; next …" --actor='<executor-actor>' --sandbox --json
```

This is an append. Do not use the replacing `--notes` field as the default
checkpoint. If nothing material changed, do not write a redundant note just to
meet a quota. Avoid credentials, raw logs, and claims unsupported by evidence.

## Capture reusable knowledge selectively

Task details and short-lived failures belong with the issue. Search existing
memory before recording a validated lesson that will likely help elsewhere.
Include its scope and evidence, use the actual executor actor for memory writes,
and amend stale knowledge intentionally. Do not save every task outcome as
global memory.

## Validate and hand off

Check the issue's acceptance conditions, run authorized relevant validation,
and record exact results. If a parent or human owns acceptance, return the
evidence without closing for them. A delegate returns attempts, results,
rationale, validation, blockers, next action, and useful record references; the
parent reconciles before continuing. If the task was an exact assignment, stop
there. Explicitly authorized batches may continue within their stated scope;
new discoveries never expand it.

When context is held or a required guarantee is missing, stop the affected path
and state the limitation. Do not switch to a manual prime, unregistered tool,
automatic setup, sync, or permission change to complete it.

## Planning and independently owned review

Follow project-owned planning and review policy. Track substantive multi-session
or delegated planning in one bounded planning item, separate from implementation;
a quick draft need not get its own ticket. Give substantive independently owned
review one bounded review item linked to planning and the exact candidate. Reuse
the same review item through corrections and rechecks. Record actual reviewer
actor/session, verdict, findings and evidence without retroactive claims.
Planning/review closure needs its own evidence and owner acceptance; readiness
alone never authorizes dispatch, implementation, release or deployment.
